nslMeaning: Standard welcoming greeting used across Nigerian deaf communities, initiated with an open flat palm gesture at temple height moving forward-outward.
description: Dominant open hand (B-handshape) begins near the side of the forehead/temple and extends smoothly outward toward the listener with a friendly facial expression.

handshape.dominant: Flat B-Hand (open 4 fingers straight, thumb resting alongside palm)

movement: Single outward forward arc, slightly opening toward partner
culturalNotes: Widely recognized in formal and informal Nigerian Deaf community settings. Often accompanied by a slight polite head nod.

metadata.verifierName: Nigerian Deaf Educational Resource Working Group
metadata.sourceOrganization: Nigerian National Association of the Deaf (NNAD) / SNEP

nslMeaning: Expression of gratitude and appreciation. In Nigerian Deaf culture, respect and gratitude are emphasized through hand-to-chin touch extending forward.
description: Fingertips of dominant flat hand touch the chin or lips and extend outward and slightly downward toward the recipient with an appreciative head tilt.
movement: Touch chin, then smooth forward descent toward conversational partner
culturalNotes: Two-handed variation is frequently used in religious, elder, or deeply respectful cultural gatherings in Nigeria.

metadata.verifierName: Nigerian Deaf Educational Resource Working Group

nslMeaning: Polite request sign, expressing courtesy and supplication.
description: Open flat palm rubs in a gentle clockwise circular motion over the center of the chest.

nonManualMarkers.facialExpression: Polite, pleading eye contact, soft brows

culturalNotes: In Nigerian Deaf context, often accompanied by a respectful upper body posture.

metadata.verifierName: Nigerian Deaf Educational Resource Working Group

signName: Bawo ni (How are you? / How are things?)
nslMeaning: Localized Nigerian informal greeting directly reflecting the Yoruba colloquial greeting 'Bawo ni' ('How are things with you?').
description: Both hands open in front of mid-chest with palms facing upward, performing a double quick wrist flick outward accompanied by inquisitive raised eyebrows.

nonManualMarkers.facialExpression: Raised eyebrows (question form), engaging head tilt

culturalNotes: Distinctive indigenous sign formation unique to the Nigerian deaf ecosystem, differing from standard ASL 'HOW ARE YOU'.

metadata.verifierName: Lagos State Deaf Association Linguistics Panel

nslMeaning: Universal urgent assistance sign used in hospital and emergency contexts.
description: Non-dominant flat palm faces upward as a base; dominant hand forms an A-fist with thumb upright on top of palm, lifting upward together toward the recipient or self depending on directionality.

handshape.dominant: Closed fist with upright thumb (A handshape)
handshape.nonDominant: Open flat palm facing upward (support base)

nonManualMarkers.facialExpression: Urgent, focused gaze; furrowed brows if requesting

culturalNotes: Highly directional verb: moving towards the signer means 'Help me'; moving toward the partner means 'I help you'.

nslMeaning: Refers to a physician or medical officer in clinics and hospitals.
description: Non-dominant arm extended forward with palm up; dominant hand's bent fingertips (M/bent hand) tap the inside of the non-dominant wrist twice, representing checking pulse.
movement: Two rhythmic taps on the radial wrist
culturalNotes: Widely standard across Nigerian hospitals and special education centers.

nslMeaning: Hospital, clinic, or medical treatment center.
description: Dominant H-hand (index and middle fingers extended together) traces a cross (+) on the upper non-dominant arm/shoulder, representing the Red Cross badge.
movement: Vertical stroke downward, followed by horizontal cross stroke
culturalNotes: Cross shape on the arm is standard across all 36 Nigerian states.

nslMeaning: Indicates physical hurt or distress at a specified anatomical location.
description: Index fingers of both hands point towards each other and perform a quick twisting motion in opposite directions near the locus of pain.
location: Near point of pain (e.g. head for headache, chest, abdomen)
movement: Opposing twisting motion towards each other twice

nonManualMarkers.facialExpression: Grimace, squinted eyes, tense mouth showing distress

culturalNotes: Facial non-manual intensity directly communicates the degree of pain to medical practitioners.

nslMeaning: Drinking water or water in general.
description: Dominant W-handshape (index, middle, and ring fingers upright) touches the index finger side against the lower lip or chin twice.

handshape.dominant: W-Hand (3 upright fingers, thumb over pinky)

movement: Two gentle taps against the lower lip
culturalNotes: Foundational survival and daily expression across all Nigerian sign dialects.

metadata.verifierName: Nigerian Deaf Educational Resource Working Group

nslMeaning: Interrogative question sign indicating location or direction inquiry.
description: Both open palms face upward in front of the body at waist height, shifting slightly from side to side with furrowed brows.

nonManualMarkers.facialExpression: Furrowed eyebrows (crucial WH-question grammar), slight head forward tilt

culturalNotes: In NSL grammar, the 'WHERE' question word is placed at the end of the sentence following the topic.

nslMeaning: Money, currency (Naira), cash payment or funds.
description: Dominant flattened O-hand/curved fingertips repeatedly tap into the upward-facing open non-dominant palm, or thumb rubs fingertips in a counting gesture.
culturalNotes: Essential for Nigerian commercial, banking, and market interactions.

metadata.verifierName: Deaf Commerce and Financial Inclusion Working Group

nslMeaning: Self-identification and community identity for deaf individuals.
description: Dominant index finger touches near the earlobe and then moves to touch near the corner of the mouth, indicating hearing and speech difference.
movement: Touch near ear, arc forward to touch near mouth
culturalNotes: Standard and affirmative term of identity within Nigerian Deaf Culture.
